DELIVERABLE: (1) Commit authors: the API passes the Slack user's mapped GitHub name and email with each prompt, and the sandbox sets `user.name` and `user.email` as separate argv values before committing. Priya's, Marco's and Dana's prompts therefore yield commits authored by each of them, not by `acme-agent`; if a Slack user has no linked GitHub identity, the API blocks that prompt's commit and asks them to link one. (2) PR opener: the API opens the PR with the GitHub token of the human who asked for it in Slack (usually Priya), not the App installation token, so the PR is authored by a person. If that user token has expired during the two-day session, the API asks the user to re-authorize in Slack and does not fall back to the app token. (3) Approval: since Priya, Marco and Dana all prompted changes, none of them should be the sole approver. Branch protection should require at least one approval from someone who did not prompt the session, and the API posts the prompter list in the PR body. (4) Handoff: the sandbox pushes only the session branch through a credential-injecting proxy outside the sandbox that mints a short-lived token scoped to that repository and branch, so no token sits in `.git/config`, the image or snapshots. After pushing, the sandbox sends the API an event with the session ID and branch name, and the API checks the branch against the session record before creating the PR. (5) Follow-ups: Marco's and Dana's later prompts restore the session snapshot, or the pushed branch if the snapshot has expired, and push to the same branch. GitHub webhooks then report PR events back to the API, which relays them to the Slack thread.
BOUNDARY: This is a design only, with no files edited. Slack-to-GitHub identity mapping, user-token storage and refresh, the exact branch-protection settings, and whether a trailer should mark agent assistance are left to implementation. The `sandbox_manager.py` template does not implement the credential proxy, snapshots or provider I/O.
EVIDENCE: Nothing was run or tested. The design follows the hosted-agents skill guidance on user-based commits, the sandbox-to-API flow, credential proxying, and snapshot expiry, applied to your Slack scenario; I did not check your repository's actual branch-protection configuration.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Rebuild the image from main on a staleness target instead of weekly: hourly 9:00-18:00 on weekdays (about 3 merges between builds at 30 merges over 9 h) and once overnight, plus an immediate rebuild when a lockfile or build config changes, with image age and failed builds alerted. (2) Claim a sandbox when the user starts typing, not on Send, so the 38 s of work runs during prompt composition, and show a visible "starting" state if it has not finished. (3) On claim, fetch and fast-forward to current main while the agent may read at once but writes stay blocked until sync completes, and run an incremental build only if the lockfile changed. (4) Replace the fixed 24/7 pool of 20 with a schedule- and demand-driven pool: size it to measured peak concurrent typing or sessions in business hours (to be measured, likely well under 40), drop to 0-2 overnight and weekends, and rely on typing-triggered warm-up for off-hours users. (5) Expire and recreate unclaimed entries whenever a new image finishes and after a maximum idle age, and release entries claimed by users who abandon the prompt. (6) Follow-up prompts restore the session snapshot, not a warm sandbox, and fall back to a fresh image plus the pushed branch if the snapshot has expired. (7) Set per-session timeouts and cost ceilings, and track image age, sync time, time to first response, pool hit rate, and merged-PR sessions.
BOUNDARY: (1) Covers warm-start policy only: image cadence, claim timing, pool sizing, sync gating, and snapshot restore. (2) Does not cover the agent loop, tool design, sub-agent topology, or client UI. (3) Pool size, rebuild interval, and idle-age limits are starting values that need tuning against measured concurrency and sync time. (4) Credentials stay in a proxy outside the sandbox, scoped to the session branch, and are not part of images or snapshots. (5) No files were edited and nothing was run.
EVIDENCE: (1) Given inputs: 38 s cold start, 40 engineers, about 30 merges per day mostly 9:00-18:00 on weekdays, weekly image, fixed pool of 20, claim on Send. (2) Derived: 30 merges over 9 h is about 3.3 per hour, so a weekly image can be on the order of 100+ merges stale and sync cost grows with that gap; the 38 s start is fully user-visible under claim-on-Send. (3) Not measured: actual peak concurrency, real sync duration, and cost, so the pool size and the benefit of hourly rebuilds are unverified and no improvement is claimed.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the fixed 24/7 pool of 20 and never refresh it; off-hours users wait for Send.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: On timeout, do NOT mark the key failed. Mark it "unknown/in_doubt" and persist, before the bank call, the key, a request fingerprint, the payout ID, and a stable bank-side idempotency reference (the same reference reused on every attempt), plus the attempt timestamp. Return 202/409-style "pending" (not 502) to the client. A retry with the same key must never issue a fresh bank payment: it first resolves the in_doubt state by querying the bank for the payout by that reference (or re-sending with the same bank idempotency reference if the bank honors it). Bank says applied → record succeeded and return the original result. Bank says not found, and only after the bank's documented window for late application has passed → record failed and allow a safe retry. Bank unreachable/unclear → stay in_doubt and return pending. Only a definitive "not applied" outcome from the bank may release the key for a new call. Run a background reconciler over in_doubt keys that polls the bank and settles them, alerting when one stays unresolved beyond a threshold. Reject same-key requests with a different fingerprint (422).

BOUNDARY: This covers the timeout handling and key state machine in POST /payouts. The proposal to lower the timeout to 5 s with exponential backoff does not fix the double payment: a shorter timeout makes late-applied requests more frequent, and backoff only spaces out retries that still issue new bank calls. Timeout tuning may be a separate latency concern. The design depends on the bank offering either a lookup by our reference or idempotent submission; I have not verified that the bank supports either, and if it supports neither, in_doubt payouts need manual or statement-based reconciliation before any retry. I edited nothing and ran nothing.

That mechanism is a timeout meaning "outcome unknown" being treated as "not applied". I have not seen the handler code, the bank API docs, or logs, and have not tested this design.
